gaps: It is the benchmark here. The weakest spot is the gold bevelled title lockup, which is closer to the key art than to the mechanism
The flat map frame is visually thinner than the 3D cogwork shots around it

tells: The palette is deliberate and unusual: dusty pink, mineral blue, olive and sea-glass green, coral, and a mauve dusk

Strong materials: translucent wax-skinned hands, glass-and-amber organic sculpture, knitted textiles, mesh, chrome tubing, beaded growths. These are complex simulations with real subsurface scattering
Every frame is a different world (landscape, volcano, sculpture, textile field, knot), yet they share one grammar, the organic grown against the synthetic
The festival-ident format justifies the small bold-sans credit tags. The OFFF MX mark is placed with intent
gaps: The typography is a plain bold sans tag dropped into the corner. It does not interact with the image, so it should be integrated, scaled or materialised into the scene

tells: The molten gold forming into regalia is a specific idea: the crown is shown being made before the title appears, which fits a show about the monarchy
Macro photography of real-looking material: oxidised bronze, gold leaf, smoke and faceted gems, with shallow depth of field and motivated low-key light
Each frame has a different scale and angle: wide smoke, a horizontal sliver, a diagonal close-up, an overhead jewel V-shape. This suggests a slow camera moving around a growing object
Small tracked Trajan-style capitals carry the credits and are placed off-axis, with the empty space around them clearly intended. The 'WITH' and the role labels follow a real credit hierarchy
On paper it fits the 'dark ground, tracked caps, serif, one accent' warning sign, but the material work and the build-to-reveal structure clearly beat that pattern
gaps: The title card returns to a centred serif on a near-empty dark ground. It is the weakest and most generic frame, and it drops the material language built up before it
The palette (black and gold) is the expected one for prestige drama, so it misses the surprise B gets from its warm parchment light and map tones
Little shifts in scale or rhythm between shots. The choreography reads as one slow tempo with no structural turn like B's mechanism-to-map moves

tells: One defining idea: the world as a clockwork map whose cities wind up out of the ground. It works as titles, as story orientation and as a symbol of the power struggle all at once
A sun-astrolabe band carved with dragon reliefs, worn wood and brass cogs, a bone-and-iron throne-tower in tilt-shift miniature. These are layered, designed props, not stock primitives

Frames move from extreme close-up on the engraved band, to a low pass over the city, to the tower rising, to an overhead parchment map, to the emblem title. The camera language and scale change deliberately
Credits sit in the world with a house-sigil glyph and engraved serif small caps. The custom title lockup is part of the emblem device
Burned-out warm sunlight against desaturated parchment and slate gives a distinctive palette that holds across all frames
gaps: The title lockup's bevelled gold treatment leans slightly towards fantasy-game convention compared with the restraint of the frames before it
The map frame flattens the lighting compared with the miniature shots, so the material richness dips for a moment
Credits are small and sometimes compete with busy detail (the Michelle Fairley card over the city), which hurts legibility in a few frames

tells: A festival-style piece in which each studio's segment is its own hybrid organism: a translucent hand holding a coral heart over a scorched ridge, glass-and-amber growths, mesh-and-fibre textile thickets, knotted tubes of jade and frosted glass
An unusual, deliberate palette that changes from section to section (blush and rust, violet dusk, cerulean, sage and peach, bottle green) yet still hangs together
Strong material simulation: subsurface scattering, frosted glass, woven mesh and fibre groom, with specular light motivated by the backgrounds
Variety between frames points to authored segments and transitions, not one template layout with the words swapped
gaps: The typography is a generic bold grotesk name tag pinned to the top-left corner, set like a lower third, with no scale contrast or connection to the image. Only the OFFF wordmark has a real point of view
No single unifying idea runs across the whole film. It reads as a showcase anthology of beautiful objects rather than one concept like B's clockwork world
Some compositions are centred-object hero renders (the mountain spire, the knot) that come close to 'effect without subject'. Each needs a narrative reason to exist in sequence

Unusual palette that changes from shot to shot: dusty rose over rust terrain, violet dusk volcano, cyan sky behind amber glass, sage green and pink fibre, bottle green with milky jade
Each frame is built differently (macro, landscape, totem, macro tangle), so it is not one layout with the words swapped
Reads as a festival title sequence with a collaborative studio credit structure (studio names as captions plus a festival wordmark lockup)
Weakness: the credit type is a plain bold grotesk dropped top-left with no integration into the image
gaps: The studio-credit typography is slide-like (small bold sans in a corner); give it a scale, placement or material relationship to the 3D worlds as B does with its engraved type

tells: A specific idea only this piece could have: the world map as a clockwork mechanism that builds itself, which states the show's politics and geography at once
Real material: tooled brass, aged parchment, an engraved astrolabe band with dragon relief, and warm sun-flare light motivated by the central sun
Strong choreography: the camera flies between cities, mechanisms unfold, and the sequence bookends on the astrolabe band that resolves into the title
Period serif credits with house sigils are set unobtrusively into the terrain, and the title lockup sits inside the astrolabe ring
Every frame works as a poster, and the dense miniature detail rewards repeat viewing
gaps: The credit type is small and sometimes illegible against busy terrain; a little more contrast control would help
The palette is mostly warm sepia and brass, and a colder accent region could add range
The final title lockup is slightly conventional (glowing trajan-like serif) next to the invention of the mechanism

tells: Macro photography of molten or cast gold forming into crown elements, with gemstone facets and pearls: a clear and fitting metaphor of the crown being forged
Excellent material rendering: specular gold, shallow focus, smoky black void, chiaroscuro light
Restrained, well-spaced classical serif credits with small-caps role labels, placed off-centre to balance the macro forms
Weakness: the dark ground, tracked serif caps and centred title on a dark ground sit close to the generic 'luxury' look, so the craft carries more than the idea does
gaps: The 'gold forming in darkness' concept is the expected answer for a royal drama; it needs a twist as specific as B's map-machine
The palette is near-monochrome gold on black, so introduce a deliberate secondary colour or tonal shift across the sequence
The final title card is a centred serif on an empty dark ground; integrate the title with the object (for example, revealed in the metal) for a memorable end beat

defects: Motion blur on the opening credit is so heavy that the name (MIRA ...) never reads cleanly in the sampled frames; the whip lands before the sign has time to read
The environment looks like a blockout: windows are flat emissive cards with no frames or depth, and the building masses are untextured boxes with murky, crushed brick
The title shot holds about 4.2s from a nearly locked camera, and the only change inside it is letters switching off
The letter dropout at the end (NIGHT HO S) reads as a random glitch, not a designed resolve
The street goes almost black between signs. Low-contrast midtones make the frames muddy rather than graphic
Chromatic fringing on the title letters is applied evenly everywhere as a filter, not motivated by light
gaps: Camera language is one repeated move: a whip-pan from sign to sign. The camera does not vary its speed, there are no reveals through depth or foreground, and nothing in the street reacts as the camera passes (no flicker-on, reflections or neighbouring signs waking up), so the walk never feels like a choreographed journey

The world is at blockout level next to top studio work. The street needs proper set dressing, wet-ground reflections, atmospheric haze, and light spilling from each sign onto the street. Right now each sign sits in a void, and that is why no single frame works as a poster

The sound is strong percussive transients plus a noise wash, with little tonal or harmonic development and no sign-specific sound design (neon hum, buzz, relay clicks). The pre-title dropout and the hit at about 8.5s are the only real dynamic moves, and the tail fades out without a sonic button that rhymes with the opening
